rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.3-2.4 and 3 - the authors run their own GIS-based multi-criteria evaluation (AHP weighting, weighted overlay) on soil, slope, land cover, distance and rainfall-deficit layers for Uganda, produce baseline and two climate-scenario suitability maps, and ground-truth the baseline map against five existing irrigation schemes (Section 3.2).
rows.notes: The study is a GIS/AHP land-suitability mapping exercise for surface irrigation in Uganda under current and projected climate. It contains no artificial intelligence, machine learning, app-based scheduling, or any learning from historical data to improve irrigation decisions; rainfall deficit is computed from 31 years of station data with CROPWAT Penman-Monteith, and factor weights come from expert consultation. It reports no result on irrigation requirements being improved, on water conservation, or on irrigation management performance/efficiency. The only link to the passage is the generic notion of supporting 'decision-making' for irrigation planning at national scale, which is a different technology (spatial suitability mapping) and a different effect (identifying suitable land) from AI-driven scheduling and water conservation. Hence Q2 is no and Q3-Q9 are no.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Supplementary tables (SM1.1-SM1.6) are referenced but not included; they would not change the ratings since the study does not address the claimed technology.
